issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-three when his Humvee hit the IED outside Kandahar. He remembers the sound—a concussive roar that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at once—and he remembers the smell of burning metal and flesh. What he does not remember, with any coherence, is what happened in the seconds immediately after. He knows his left leg was fractured in two places. He knows Sergeant Rivera, who had been sitting across from him, took shrapnel to the abdomen and died before the medevac arrived. He knows he was conscious enough to see Rivera's blood pooling beneath him on the metal floor, but when Marcus tries to recall the exact sequence of events, the memory fractures into disconnected pieces that refuse to fit together—a flash of Rivera's face, a sensation of heat, a noise like screaming, but no coherent narrative that feels real. Even now, five years later, the memory is so extreme, so divorced from the orderly way his mind expects events to unfold, that part of him struggles to believe it actually happened to him. It feels more like something he watched in a film, something that happened to someone else.

Marcus left the service at twenty-five with a medical discharge and a Purple Heart. He settled in Portland with his girlfriend, Sasha, and took a job as a social media manager at a mid-sized marketing firm. To anyone watching, his recovery looked straightforward. He went to physical therapy, regained full mobility in his leg, and seemed to move forward. But in the years since, Marcus has come to believe something fundamental and unchangeable has shattered inside him. He is permanently damaged now, altered in ways he cannot repair, and this conviction shapes how he interprets every moment of difficulty. When he struggles to fall asleep at night—lying rigid in bed, ears attuned to every sound in the apartment, body tense as though bracing for impact—he understands it as proof of his permanent alteration. He needs to stay alert, to monitor his environment, because his nervous system no longer works the way it should. Other men, men who hadn't been in that Humvee, would sleep soundly. They would not be permanently changed like this.

The triggers that set off his hypervigilance are specific and unforgiving. Helicopter sounds—the distinctive thump of rotor blades, whether from a news helicopter overhead or an emergency medical flight passing near the city—send a jolt of adrenaline through his chest that makes his heart race and his palms sweat. The sight of visible injuries on others, even minor ones, can trigger an overwhelming physical reaction: his breathing becomes shallow, his muscles tighten, and he feels a surge of panic that seems entirely disproportionate to what he is actually seeing. And driving with other people in the car—a seemingly ordinary activity—has become fraught with danger in his mind. When Sasha sits beside him in traffic, or when he carpools with colleagues to a work event, Marcus finds himself hypervigilant, scanning the road ahead, bracing for something catastrophic. These triggers activate a cascade of threat responses: his body becomes flooded with the physical sensations of danger, his startle reflex becomes hair-trigger sensitive, and he finds himself reacting with alarm when Sasha touches his shoulder unexpectedly or when a coworker brushes past him in the hallway. The fragmented memories of the explosion—those disconnected pieces that refuse to cohere—seem to activate simultaneously, flooding him with the raw emotional intensity of the event even without any clear image of what he is remembering.

To manage these eruptions, Marcus has developed a careful architecture of avoidance and control. He rehearses conversations before any interaction, running through multiple scenarios in his mind to anticipate what might be said and how he should respond, because spontaneous social exchange feels dangerously unpredictable. He avoids situations that put his body under physical stress—he stopped going to the gym, stopped playing the pickup basketball he once loved, stopped anything that elevates his heart rate—because he cannot distinguish between the normal acceleration of his pulse during exercise and the terrifying surge of panic that accompanies his triggers. He will not watch films or television shows that depict violence or injury, and he crosses the street to avoid storefronts with military or police uniforms in the window displays. These avoidance strategies provide temporary relief; in the moment of dodging a trigger, Marcus feels safer. But the relief is short-lived and comes at a cost. By avoiding situations that stress his body, he has become deconditioned and more physically reactive to minor stressors. By rehearsing conversations obsessively, he has become so self-conscious in social interaction that he appears stilted and anxious to others, which reinforces his conviction that he is an outsider, fundamentally different from people who have not experienced trauma. His avoidance behaviors have also begun to erode his relationship with Sasha. She has stopped asking him to drive with her anywhere, stopped inviting him to social events where he might encounter unexpected triggers, and though she does not say so directly, Marcus can feel her frustration accumulating. Last month, when she suggested he might benefit from therapy, he heard it as confirmation that he is broken in ways she cannot accept.

The fragmented memories themselves seem to perpetuate the cycle. When Marcus experiences a flashback—not a clear cinematic replay, but rather a sudden overwhelming flood of the emotional terror of that moment, divorced from any coherent image—he responds by tightening his grip on control. He rehearses conversations even more obsessively, avoids even more situations, stays more vigilant at night. The disconnected pieces of memory, the emotional intensity without narrative structure, convince him that his mind is fundamentally damaged, that he cannot trust his own processing, and this belief makes him more hypervigilant, more prone to interpreting ambiguous stimuli as threats. When he hears a helicopter in the distance, the fragmented memory activates, and he finds himself bracing for the impact, certain that something terrible is about to happen. When he sees a colleague's bandaged hand in the office, the memory floods him with panic, and he interprets the experience as evidence that he is permanently altered, that other people would not react this way. The negative appraisals—the certainty that he is permanently damaged, that someone else would not have gotten into the situation that led to his trauma, that he is now an outsider to normal human experience—seem to sharpen his threat detection. He becomes more alert to potential dangers, more likely to notice things that could hurt him, more convinced that the world is fundamentally unsafe.

Marcus is twenty-eight now, and the architecture of avoidance has become so elaborate that it has begun to collapse under its own weight. He called his therapist three weeks ago, on a Tuesday evening after Sasha had gone to bed, because he realized he could no longer drive anywhere alone without being seized by panic. The thought of being behind the wheel, responsible for navigating traffic, vulnerable to the sudden appearance of injuries or the unexpected sound of aircraft overhead, has become unbearable. He does not yet know if therapy will help him rebuild the narrative of what happened that day, or if it will help him tolerate the fragmented, overwhelming emotional reality of his memories. What he knows is that he cannot continue like this—trapped between the conviction that he is permanently broken and the desperate, unspoken hope that perhaps, somehow, he is not.
